> **Q2：Details on Model Computation, Memory Usage, and Latency**

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion.

We provide a detailed analysis of the computational complexity of the LLaVA-RadZ framework, summarizing training time under different strategies.  The results are presented in the following table:

|                           | **LLaVA-Med** | **LLaVA-RadZ**（wo/DKAM） | LLaVA-RadZ |
| ------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------- | ---------- |
| Training Cost (GPU-hours) | 32.80         | 33.89                     | 34.26      |

Under identical hardware configurations (2 × A100 80GB GPUs) and training settings, our method introduces only **~4.5%** additional training cost compared with the LLaVA-Med baseline. This minimal overhead leads to a clear gain in zero-shot generalization performance, demonstrating a favorable balance between efficiency and effectiveness.

In terms of inference efficiency, LLaVA-RadZ exhibits even more significant advantages. The per-sample computational cost is approximately **4329.26 GFLOPs**, considerably lower than the baseline’s **5122.74 GFLOPs**. Additionally, the average inference latency is reduced from **539.3 ms** to **95.4 ms**, achieving a **5.6× speedup**. These results collectively indicate that the proposed training strategies not only strengthen semantic alignment and domain knowledge integration but also substantially improve overall computational efficiency. Therefore, our framework offers strong practical potential for real-world deployment.

> **Q3：Fine-tuning Details**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

All baseline models and our proposed method follow the **same training protocol**, and are trained exclusively on the **same source dataset, MIMIC-CXR**. Throughout training, **none of the models were exposed to any samples from downstream target datasets** (e.g., RSNA, COVIDx, etc.). During evaluation, all models are assessed under an identical **zero-shot setting** on the same target datasets.

> **Q4：Target Dataset Anchor Generation**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

Please refer to our response to **W2**, where we provide a detailed explanation of how dataset-specific semantic anchors are generated during both the training and inference phases.

> **Q5：Sensitivity Analysis of Prompts, Anchor Length, and Generative Model Choice**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

In our preliminary exploration, we experimented with several prompt templates. We found that **free-form generative instructions** often introduced excessive randomness into the generated content, leading to noticeable instability in model performance. To ensure consistency and semantic precision, we adopted a unified, structured prompt template:

```
Describe the key characteristics of [Disease] in terms of pathophysiology, imaging findings, and clinical manifestations.
```

We further constrained the description length to **within 100 words**. When descriptions became excessively long, we observed that additional irrelevant details introduced noise, causing slight performance degradation. Regarding the choice of the generative model, LLaVA-RadZ exhibited **moderate sensitivity** to the quality of generated descriptions, indicating that our method maintains reasonable robustness while still benefiting from higher-quality text. In principle, employing a stronger and more stable LLM is expected to yield **better and more reproducible disease descriptions**, which can further enhance overall performance.

> **Q6： Handling Label Space Shift**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

It is important to emphasize that **COVID-19 does not appear in the MIMIC-CXR training data**, and therefore its description **is not involved in any part of the training process**. Nonetheless, our model still demonstrates strong generalization capability on this unseen category. This effect does not arise from any form of targeted label engineering; rather, it is a direct result of the model’s **learned cross-modal semantic alignment ability**, which enables it to effectively project the description of an unseen disease into semantically related regions within the learned representation space.

> **Q7：Strategy for Ontology Mismatch**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

Please refer to our response to **W2**, where we clarified that, in order to address potential mismatches, we adopted a **unified and generalizable template** for constructing textual descriptions.

>  **W1:  Motivation and Novelty**

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments.

Our work is motivated by addressing the fundamental limitations of existing large models in zero-shot medical image classification. To this end, we introduce a **lightweight and relatively decoupled adaptation framework**, which—unlike existing approaches that rely on full-model fine-tuning or complex prompt engineering—aims to **activate the intrinsic cross-modal generalization capabilities of MLLMs without disrupting their original semantic space**. By incorporating DFAT and DKAM, our framework improves alignment and knowledge utilization while maintaining architectural simplicity.

To the best of our knowledge, **this is the first exploration of a decoupled adaptation paradigm specifically designed for zero-shot medical image classification within the domain of medical vision–language models**. Therefore, we believe that our method represents a clear **methodological novelty and forward-looking contribution**, rather than a minor incremental improvement.

More importantly, given the rapid advancement of foundational MLLMs, our framework exhibits a distinct **evolutionary advantage**: its performance naturally scales with the strength of the underlying base model. This provides a **sustainable and scalable pathway** toward overcoming the performance bottlenecks of large models in fine-grained medical image analysis.

> **W2:  Necessity of Classification Tasks and Future Potential of the Model**

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments.

Our decision to focus on zero-shot medical image classification is driven by practical clinical considerations. In real-world medical scenarios, models must be capable of recognizing previously unseen conditions—such as emerging diseases, rare disorders, or cases where annotated data is scarce. This makes zero-shot learning not only relevant, but essential for building clinically reliable and adaptable AI systems.

It is also important to highlight that medical image diagnosis is inherently a **multimodal reasoning process**. Effective interpretation requires more than recognizing visual patterns; the model must understand the semantic relationships between medical concepts, connect imaging findings to underlying pathophysiology, and integrate heterogeneous clinical information. This capability of cross-modal semantic alignment and medical reasoning is precisely where large multimodal models offer advantages over traditional vision-only architectures.

We also emphasize that the potential of large multimodal models in medical image classification remains largely underexplored. The gap between theoretical expectations and current empirical performance is a key motivation behind our work. We argue that research should not remain constrained within the paradigm of conventional visual feature extractors (e.g., ViT-based models). Instead, it is crucial to explore the new opportunities enabled by MLLMs in this domain.

Our proposed vision–language pretraining alignment framework represents a step in this direction. By leveraging the intrinsic reasoning capacity of large models, it serves as an effective means to expand their capability boundaries—particularly for fine-grained and clinically complex classification tasks.

summary.value:
The paper proposes LLaVA-RadZ, a framework designed to enhance zero-shot medical image recognition using multimodal large language models (MLLMs). It introduces two main components:

First, DFAT, which extracts and aligns multimodal features from the decoder side using specially designed tokens <ImgCls> and <TxtCls>.

Second DKAM: which integrates domain-specific semantic anchors generated from medical knowledge to guide cross-modal alignment.

The motivation is to bridge the performance gap between generative MLLMs and discriminative vision-language models in medical zero-shot settings.

strengths.value:
1. Reasonable token design.
The introduction of <ImgCls> and <TxtCls> tokens is intuitive and aligns well with the goal of disentangling modality-specific information. The authors provide convincing evidence via clustering analysis and ablations, though I would appreciate more direct visualization of attention distributions to confirm that these tokens truly capture the intended modality cues.

2. Concept-level extraction of medical knowledge.
The DKAM module essentially performs a structured concept extraction and anchoring step for medical entities, which is conceptually coherent and consistent with similar attempts in recent multimodal medical reasoning works.

weaknesses.value:
1. Performing zero-shot classification using MLLMs is a rather niche setting. In realistic medical scenarios, simpler and far more efficient CNN or vision transformer models would be more appropriate and interpretable for image classification tasks. Thus, the motivation for adapting a large MLLM to this task feels weak.

2. Using contrastive learning for adaptation appears superficial for an MLLM. Given that token-level tuning or adapter-based fine-tuning is feasible, the proposed approach feels like an indirect workaround rather than a deep integration into the model’s architecture.

3. The reported gains (e.g., in Table 2) are marginal compared to recent state-of-the-art classification models. The improvements, while consistent, are not substantial enough to justify the added complexity and computational cost of the proposed framework.

> **W1: Model Generalization Evaluation**

We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback.

We further evaluated our model on additional types of medical imaging datasets, including CT scans, MRI datasets, and X-ray datasets involving other disease types, such as the Chest CT-Scan Dataset [1], Brain Tumor MRI Dataset [2], and InBreast Mammography Dataset [3]. As the experiments demonstrate, although LLaVA-RadZ is trained solely on chest-related datasets, it still exhibits improved cross-task generalization capabilities. Compared with chest radiography, its performance on datasets involving different disease categories and imaging modalities is relatively less pronounced. We attribute this primarily to the limitations imposed by the training data distribution. We hypothesize that incorporating a wider range of disease categories and a larger-scale training corpus into LLaVA-RadZ would lead to more substantial performance gains.

Nonetheless, the current results already provide strong evidence that, compared with conventional fine-tuning paradigms, the proposed DFAT training strategy can effectively leverage features extracted by large multimodal models to address complex recognition tasks, and importantly, this capability generalizes across domains.

> **W2: Sensitivity Analysis of Model Fine-tuning**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions.

The core contribution of our framework lies in proposing a more effective vision–language pretraining alignment strategy. Unlike many existing approaches that require **task-specific fine-tuning on downstream datasets** to adapt to new tasks, our method is designed to achieve strong **zero-shot generalization** through pretraining solely on an initial dataset (MIMIC-CXR). To validate this capability, we adopt a rigorous zero-shot evaluation protocol: the model is pretrained only on MIMIC-CXR and then directly evaluated on multiple large-scale radiology diagnosis datasets (including RSNA, SIIM-ACR, and COVIDx CXR-2). It is important to emphasize that these downstream datasets exhibit substantial distributional differences from MIMIC-CXR, and the disease categories in COVIDx CXR-2 are entirely unseen during pretraining.

As shown in Table 1, under this highly challenging **pure zero-shot setting**, our method substantially outperforms baseline models that are trained on the same pretraining data and evaluated on the same downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner. These results strongly demonstrate that our proposed pretraining and alignment strategy enables the model to learn more generalizable vision–language representations, thereby improving its ability to handle unseen data and previously unseen diseases.

This paper introduces the LLaVA-RadZ framework, a novel approach to zero-shot medical disease recognition using Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Despite the impressive performance of MLLMs in general tasks, the paper identifies that they struggle with fine-grained medical image recognition, particularly in radiology disease classification, due to issues with feature extraction and alignment between images and corresponding medical texts.

The paper proposes LLaVA-RadZ as a solution, which includes several innovative components:

Decoding-Side Feature Alignment Training (DFAT): A strategy designed to leverage the strengths of the MLLM decoder architecture by introducing special tokens for image and text modalities. This enables the effective extraction of global representations from both the image and the text.

Domain Knowledge Anchoring Module (DKAM): This module utilizes the inherent medical knowledge within the model to enhance the understanding of medical diseases and bridge the semantic gap between images and text descriptions. It helps align image-text pairs based on disease categories.

Cross-modal Contrastive Loss: To further improve the alignment between image and text features, this loss function optimizes both global and local feature representations across modalities.

strengths.value:
Innovative Framework: The LLaVA-RadZ framework introduces a novel approach to zero-shot medical disease recognition by leveraging MLLM features directly. The inclusion of DFAT and DKAM for enhancing cross-modal alignment is a strong contribution, as it enables the model to utilize its inherent capabilities without task-specific fine-tuning.

Strong Results: The experiments provide compelling evidence that the LLaVA-RadZ model significantly outperforms traditional models, such as CLIP and other state-of-the-art methods, in various disease recognition tasks. This includes improved accuracy and F1 scores across multiple medical datasets, showcasing the model’s potential in practical medical applications.

Domain Knowledge Integration: The integration of domain-specific medical knowledge through the DKAM module effectively bridges the gap between image and text data, improving both feature alignment and category-level understanding. This enhances the robustness and interpretability of the model in medical contexts.

Scalability and Generalization: The framework’s ability to work in zero-shot settings and generalize across various medical disease datasets without requiring extensive labeled data makes it highly valuable for real-world medical applications, where such datasets are often limited.

weaknesses.value:
Limited Domain Coverage: While the framework performs well on several benchmark datasets, a broader evaluation on other medical imaging datasets (e.g., CT scans, MRIs) or more diverse diseases would strengthen the claims about the generalizability of the model across different medical conditions.

Fine-Tuning Sensitivity: Although the framework shows improvement over standard methods, it still relies on fine-tuning to achieve the best results. A deeper exploration of how the model behaves in pure zero-shot settings without any fine-tuning would be beneficial, especially in terms of robustness to unseen diseases or rare conditions.

Model Complexity and Efficiency: While the results are promising, the computational complexity of the LLaVA-RadZ framework, particularly the use of multiple training strategies (DFAT, DKAM, contrastive loss), should be better analyzed. Understanding the trade-off between model complexity and performance is important for real-world deployment.

Interpretability: While the framework offers improved feature alignment, more explicit methods to interpret the model’s decision-making process could increase trust in clinical settings. Providing visualization tools or methods to explain how image features and text descriptions are aligned could further enhance the framework's usability.

summary.value: The paper introduces **LLaVA-RadZ** which is a medical multi-modal large language model for zero-shot radiology disease recognition by mining the decoder’s penultimate-layer features with special tokens (global + local) and aligning them via symmetric cross-modal InfoNCE (**DFAT**). It further adds a **Domain Knowledge Anchor Module (DKAM)** that uses LLM-written disease descriptions as category prototypes, pulling image/text features toward disease-level semantics. On several chest X-ray benchmarks, the method is competitive with CLIP-style baselines in zero/low-shot settings and remains strong with 1% labeled data.

strengths.value:
1) **DFAT**: Add modality-specific special tokens (⟨ImgCls⟩/⟨TxtCls⟩), extract penultimate-layer embeddings as global features, pool the rest as local features, and train with symmetric global and local InfoNCE to align image-text pairs.

2) **DKAM**:  Auto-generate disease descriptions with the LLM and map them into a semantic vector set; add a category-guided contrastive loss so image/text features align at the disease-category level.

3) **Novelty**: the proposed method improves MLLMs with SOTA CLIP-style models for zero-shot CXR classification

weaknesses.value:
1) **Domain scope is narrow**: the study provides results for chest X-ray only. There is no CT, MRI, ultrasound, so the generalization of radiology data (including X-ray, CT, utrasound) is unproven.

2) **Zero-shot protocol**: the paper mainly focus on the capacity of **DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE ANCHOR MODULE**. However, the protocol for label mapping are unclear. For examples, **RSNA Pneumonia** is a single binary label dataset, how to mapping from the pre-trained anchors to the target labels set. Additionally, COVIDx CXR-2 is collected from COVID-19 patients which does not have compatible labels with classic pneumonia. How does the proposed method generate anchors or mapping labels across datasets? Zero-shot performances heavily depend on what labels are used for training. If the target labels are used for training, that is **target-aware labels supervision**.

3) **Goal clarity**: the proposed method focus on enhance one ability of MLLM for one data modality, instead of improve the general abilities of MLLM for one specific disease or image modality. For a **radiology** MLLM meant to answer all relevant CXR questions such as grading, disease recognition, localization, or generating report or answer VQA questions. Please clarify your goal?

4) **Interpretability**: the proposed method does not provide explanation or evidence localization. for the final diagnosis. In clinic setting, the explanation or evidence is very important for radiologist review.

> **Q1：Sensitivity Analysis on Number of Special Tokens and Hidden Layer Depth**

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion.

This suggests that an appropriate number of special tokens enhances the model’s ability to allocate attention across different semantic regions, whereas an excessively small or large number of tokens adversely impacts representation efficiency.

Regarding hidden layer depth, we observe that **the model achieves the best performance when extracting features from the second-to-last layer**. We attribute this to the **complementarity of representational hierarchies**. In Transformer-based architectures, the final layer tends to produce highly abstract, task-specific representations, while the penultimate layer retains richer local details and structured information. For fine-grained medical image classification tasks, these mid-level representations offer a more balanced semantic encoding.

 Here, *[Disease]* is replaced only with entity categories present in MIMIC-CXR.

During training, the generated disease descriptions are encoded into a **knowledge-vector repository**. Using a contrastive learning mechanism, the model aligns medical images and their corresponding reports with the correct disease-description vectors in the semantic space, while simultaneously pushing them away from irrelevant descriptions. This enables the model to learn highly discriminative cross-modal representations.

During inference, we construct a corresponding description set according to the label system of the target dataset. For entities already included in the training knowledge base (e.g., “pneumonia” in RSNA), we directly use their pre-learned vector representations. For unseen entities (e.g., COVID-19), we employ a neutral descriptive template such as **“Chest X-ray showing {class_name}”** to serve as their semantic representation. All candidate descriptions are fed as text-side inputs, and zero-shot classification is performed by computing their similarity to the query image in the aligned embedding space.

Importantly, since COVID-19 does not appear in the MIMIC-CXR training samples, its description is not used during model training. Nevertheless, the model still demonstrates strong generalization ability. For binary-classification tasks such as RSNA Pneumonia, the problem is formulated as semantic matching between the anchors “pneumonia” and “non-pneumonia.” This behavior is not due to specially engineered labels; rather, it emerges naturally from the cross-modal semantic alignment learned by the model, which enables previously unseen disease descriptions to be effectively projected into the appropriate regions of the learned semantic space.

summary.value: This paper proposes LLaVA-RadZ, a simple framework for zero-shot radiology disease recognition that leverages medical MLLM-based features instead of the standard VQA pipeline.

strengths.value:
1. The paper has a clear and coherent narrative flow: it starts from the problem formulation, introduces the proposed method, and then validates it through extensive experiments. 
2. The experimental results are well-presented and show competitive performance. 
3. The method is also evaluated on multiple datasets, together with thorough ablation studies to justify the design choices.

weaknesses.value:
1. The methodological novelty is relatively narrow. The framework mainly adapts an existing MLLM with feature-alignment tricks and prompt tokens for zero-shot classification, which feels incremental rather than conceptually new. The core idea—repurposing MLLM features for contrastive alignment—is more of an engineering extension than a fundamentally new direction.
2. The problem formulation underutilizes the capacity of modern MLLMs. Given that MLLMs are designed for rich medical reasoning and compositional understanding, constraining such a large model to a basic zero-shot disease classification task seems mismatched with its strengths and does not convincingly motivate why MLLM reasoning ability is necessary here.
3. Fairness of comparison remains unclear. The parameter scale of MLLMs is fundamentally different from CLIP-based baselines, making the comparison difficult to interpret. The gains reported against optimized medical CLIP-style models (e.g., MAVL) are often modest or inconsistent across datasets, and in some cases marginal in absolute terms, which raises questions about practical significance and whether the additional model complexity is justified.
4. From a clinical utility perspective, the improvements may be limited. The work focuses on common radiology benchmarks rather than clinically high-value or safety-critical scenarios, and several metrics exhibit only small deltas over strong prior art. Without demonstrating improved interpretability, robustness, or real-world benefit, the incremental accuracy gains translate weakly to actionable clinical impact.
5. The computational and training overhead is non-trivial. Leveraging a full MLLM backbone and LoRA finetuning introduces substantial resource cost compared to more lightweight radiology-specific encoders. The paper lacks a clear cost–benefit discussion, and the additional complexity may not justify the marginal performance improvements for practical deployment settings.

> **Q8：Clarification on Anchor Sources and Training Protocol**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

In our study, the construction of disease descriptions is strictly based on the **label space of the pre-training dataset (MIMIC-CXR)**. We generate semantic anchors only for disease entities that appear in MIMIC-CXR. To ensure consistency and avoid variations caused by free-form generation, we employ a single structured prompt template:

> **Q9：Ablation Study and Analysis of Temperature Parameter**

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments.

The temperature parameter (τ) plays a critical role in our contrastive learning objective by controlling the “sharpness” of the similarity distribution. To thoroughly assess its impact, we conducted a systematic ablation study, summarized as follows:

|    τ     | RSNA-Pneumonia (F1) | SIIM-ACR (F1) |
| :------: | :-----------------: | :-----------: |
|   0.01   |        73.54        |     74.81     |
|   0.03   |        74.90        |     77.21     |
| **0.05** |      **76.18**      |     79.57     |
|   0.07   |        75.99        |   **79.58**   |
|   0.10   |        75.84        |     78.81     |

We evaluated five values of **τ**, ranging from 0.01 to 0.10, on two datasets, **RSNA-Pneumonia** and **SIIM-ACR**, using **macro F1** as the primary evaluation metric. All other hyperparameters were kept constant to ensure a fair comparison. Based on the results, we selected **τ = 0.05** as the default value for all experiments, as it provides the **best balance between discriminative power and generalization performance**. The effectiveness of this choice was further confirmed by consistent improvements observed across multiple zero-shot multi-class classification benchmarks.
